title: Fan out with coroutines, inside a deadline
goal: By the end you can fan one price request out to three couriers with `async` inside `supervisorScope`, give every call the same deadline with `withTimeoutOrNull`, fall back to the last good price marked stale, and tie each request's coroutine to its connection with `scope.future { }`, so that a client who hangs up cancels the courier calls.
opening:
Remember the home cook from the Kotlin coroutines track. When she needed tomatoes, she texted three shops at once and waited only as long as the slowest reply. Now she does it for the post office counter. A customer asks what it costs to send a parcel to Lisbon. She texts three couriers, sets the kitchen timer, and passes on the cheapest reply that came in before it rang.

The plan is simple, and a bad day breaks it in three places. One courier answers with an error, and a careless kitchen throws away the other two replies. One is still typing when the timer rings. And the customer may walk away before anyone answers, leaving three couriers working for nobody.

A Netty server that never blocks its loop left the counter with a promise: `quote` hands back a ticket at once. In this lesson, we'll keep that promise with coroutines: ask all three couriers together under one deadline, let one fail alone, serve the last good price when nobody answers, and stop the calls when the customer hangs up. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: Inside `coroutineScope { }`, three `async` calls ask three couriers for a price. One courier throws `IOException` after 50 ms; the other two would answer at 120 and 300 ms. What does the request get?
options: The lower of the two prices that came back, after 300 ms
The `IOException` after about 50 ms, and the other two calls are cancelled
The `IOException` after 300 ms, once the other two calls have finished
Two prices and a `null` for the courier that failed
warmup.why: A failed child cancels its parent at once, and a plain scope then cancels the other children and rethrows. So the request fails at 50 ms with the `IOException`, and the two calls that would have answered are cancelled. That's right when you need every answer, and wrong when any one will do. The fix for a price is `supervisorScope`, this lesson's first change.

sections.h: When nobody answers, serve the last good price and say it is stale
sections.body:
Sometimes no courier answers by the deadline. The network between us and them is down, or every courier is swamped on the busiest morning of the year. The service then has three choices. It can wait longer, fail the request, or serve the last price it saw.

Waiting longer breaks the deadline, which is the one promise the service makes. Failing is honest, and no help to a customer who only wants a rough idea of the cost. So `BestQuote` keeps a **cache**, a store of recent answers kept close at hand: here, the last live price for each destination. When nobody answers, it serves that price marked as **stale**, old and labelled so, as `7 STALE LISBON 12.41 eastgate`. The customer sees the word and decides whether a slightly old price is good enough:

```kotlin
val best = answers.minByOrNull { it.price }
if (best != null) {
    cache.remember(best)                       // only live answers refresh the cache
    return best
}
return cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale()  // an old price, marked, beats no price
    ?: throw NoQuoteException(destination)     // the handler writes "7 ERR no quote for LISBON"
```

```java
// Java equivalent with Reactor: an empty Optional switches to the cache
.flatMap(best -> best.map(Mono::just).orElseGet(() -> fromCache(destination)))
.doOnNext(q -> { if (!q.stale()) cache.remember(q); })   // only live answers refresh the cache
```

Two rules keep the cache honest. Only live answers go into it. If a stale answer could refresh the cache, one old price could be served forever, each serving making it look new. And with nothing cached, the request fails with `NoQuoteException`, which lesson 1's handler turns into `7 ERR no quote for LISBON`. A shrug, but at least a quick one. A production cache would also have an age limit, so that a price from a minute ago is served and one from last week is not.

Check yourself: after an outage, the couriers recover. On the next request Eastgate answers 12.39 and Fjord 12.42. What does the customer get, and what does the cache hold for Lisbon afterwards? (`OK LISBON 12.39 eastgate`, and the cache now holds that live price in place of the old one.)

The fan-out is complete. It still has to meet lesson 1's Java handler, and the handler holds the one thing we haven't used yet: a cancel.

aside.title: Is serving an old price honest?
aside.body: It is when it says so. The reply carries the word `STALE`, so the customer, or the program they use, knows the price may have moved and can decide. For a rough idea of the cost, a recent price is fine; for a booking, the courier will confirm the real price anyway. What would not be honest is serving the old price as `OK`. That's why the label lives in the `Quote` itself, as its `stale` field, and the protocol turns it into a different word on the wire.

compare.title: The fan-out with Reactor's Mono.zip and with coroutines

java.title: BestQuoteReactor.java

kotlin.title: BestQuote.kt

compare.note: Both start the three calls together, give each its own deadline, turn a failure into "no answer", keep the lowest price and fall back to the cache. In Reactor, every outcome becomes a value at the source. A timeout is an error signal you resume from, and an empty source is a third outcome you must name with `defaultIfEmpty`, or `Mono.zip` completes empty (Combining streams: zip, merge, concat, combineLatest). Nothing runs until something subscribes, and cancelling the subscription cancels the three calls. In Kotlin, the same policy is ordinary control flow: a scope, `try` and `catch`, `minByOrNull`. The scope guarantees that when `quote` returns, every call is either done or cancelled. The price of that directness is the `CancellationException` rule, which only coroutines have: a timeout is a cancel, so you must tell your own cancel from a courier's.

worked.title: Test the deadline and the hang-up on virtual time

steps.say: Make the couriers controllable on the test clock. `delay` inside `runTest` uses virtual time, so a fake that delays 1,000 ms costs nothing, and recording cancellations in the `catch` tells the test exactly who was stopped.

Test the deadline. `currentTime` is the virtual clock, so the assertion can be exact: 300, not "under 400". A version on the real clock would take 300 ms per test and could fail on a busy build machine.

Test the hang-up through `QuoteService`. Pass `StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)` as its context, and the service's own scope runs on the test clock too. `runCurrent()` runs what is due now, without moving the clock.

Know where virtual time stops. A `delay` inside `withContext(Dispatchers.Default)` escapes the test scheduler and takes real time (Shared state and testing coroutines), which is why the service takes its dispatcher as a parameter. The two end-to-end tests in this lab use `Dispatchers.Default` and a real Netty server, so they assert only with latches: 6 courier calls started, 6 cancelled after the hang-up. Self-check: what would `currentTime` read in a test that built `QuoteService(Dispatchers.Default, ...)` inside `runTest`? (0: the coroutines ran on real threads, and the virtual clock never moved.)

lab.title: Fan out to three couriers, and cancel on hang-up
steps: Run the tests. Ten of eleven fail. The Java files in `l02` are lesson 1's solution, carried over; the tests' couriers are in `src/test/.../l02/FakeProvider.kt`.
Fix `BestQuote` along points 1 to 3 of its KDoc: `supervisorScope`, `withTimeoutOrNull` inside each `async`, and an await that turns failures into `null` and rethrows only your own cancel.
Add point 4: remember the best live price, else serve `cache.lastGood(destination)?.asStale()`, else throw `NoQuoteException(destination)`. The six `BestQuote` tests should pass.
Write `QuoteService`: a private scope from `context + SupervisorJob()`, `quote` with `scope.future { }`, `inFlight` from the scope's job, and `close`.
Run the tests until all eleven pass, including the two over TCP. Run them once more.
hints: If the deadline test fails with `TimeoutCancellationException: Timed out after 300ms of _virtual_ ... time`, you still use `withTimeout`, or you rethrow every `CancellationException`.
`supervisorScope` returns what its block returns. Map the deferreds to `awaitOrNull()` inside the block, and `filterNotNull()` outside it.
`scope.future { }` is in `kotlinx.coroutines.future`. It starts the coroutine on the scope's dispatcher and returns the future at once.
`inFlight` is `scope.coroutineContext.job.children.count()`; `job` is an extension property from `kotlinx.coroutines`.
lab.done_when: All eleven tests in `FanOutTest` pass, twice in a row.

drill.title: Write the best-of fan-out from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `BestQuote.quote(destination)` from memory: all couriers at once, the same deadline for each, a failed or late courier counts as no answer, your own cancel still propagates, the lowest price wins, and with no answer you serve the cached price as stale or throw `NoQuoteException`. Which line would break the request when a courier's own client times out?

recap: Fan out with `async` inside a scope: three couriers at 120, 300 and 200 ms answer in 300 ms instead of 620.
Give each call the deadline with `withTimeoutOrNull`. A late courier drops out as `null` and the others still count; one timeout around the whole fan-out throws away answers that already arrived.

`supervisorScope` lets each courier fail alone, and a courier's own timeout is a `CancellationException` too. In the catch, `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` rethrows only if your coroutine was cancelled.
With no answer, serve the last live price marked `STALE`, or fail with `NoQuoteException`. Only live answers refresh the cache.

`scope.future { }` gives the Java handler a future at once, and cancelling it cancels the request's coroutine and its courier calls. The scope uses `SupervisorJob`, so one failed request can't cancel the others.
Where today's service stops: every request still goes to every courier at once, with no limit. A thousand requests mean a thousand calls to each courier.
closing:
We started with a cook texting three couriers, the kitchen timer running, and a customer who might walk away. Now every request asks all three at once under one deadline. A courier that fails or runs late drops out alone, an old price goes out only with its label, and a hang-up reaches every pot on the stove.

Now look in your own code for `coroutineScope` around calls where any one answer would do, and for `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` around an `await`.

Next, we'll put the service under load. What happens when a thousand customers ask at once, and Northline's contract allows only ten calls at a time?

quiz.q: Inside `supervisorScope`, an `async` child throws `IOException` at 50 ms, while its two siblings run until 300 ms. Nobody has called `await` yet. What happens at 50 ms?
options: The scope is cancelled and rethrows the `IOException`
Nothing visible: the exception waits in that child's `Deferred`, and the siblings keep running
The uncaught exception handler prints it, and the siblings are cancelled
The two siblings are cancelled, but the scope itself keeps running
quiz.why: In a supervisor, a failed child doesn't cancel its siblings or the scope. A failed `async` keeps its exception for `await`, which rethrows it when you get there. A handler is never used for `async`. In a plain `coroutineScope`, the first option would be right.

quiz.q: Each courier call is `async { withTimeout(300) { c.quote(d) } }` inside `supervisorScope`, and the code that awaits it does `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }`. One courier takes a second. What does the request get?
options: The best of the other two prices, with `null` for the slow courier
It waits a full second for the slow courier
An `IOException` from the slow courier
It ends with `TimeoutCancellationException`, as if the whole request had been cancelled
quiz.why: `withTimeout` signals a late call with `TimeoutCancellationException`, a subclass of `CancellationException`. The catch rethrows it, so one courier's timeout ends the request. Use `withTimeoutOrNull` for your own deadline, and call `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` before deciding a cancel was yours.

quiz.q: In the Reactor version, one courier's `Mono` completes empty: no value and no error. What does `Mono.zip` of the three do if that source has no `defaultIfEmpty`?
options: It emits a tuple with an empty slot
It fails with `NoSuchElementException`
It completes empty at once and cancels the other two calls
It waits for the other two and emits their pair
quiz.why: `Mono.zip` needs one value from every source. When one completes empty there is nothing to combine, so the zip completes empty, with no error, and cancels the rest. The request would get no price and no error. Mapping each source to `Optional` with `defaultIfEmpty(Optional.empty())` names the empty case.

quiz.q: `QuoteService.quote` returned `scope.future { best.quote(destination) }` to the handler, and the client hangs up, so `channelInactive` calls `cancel(true)` on it. What happens to the three courier calls?
options: They are cancelled at their next suspension point: cancelling the future cancels the coroutine, and the cancel goes down the job tree
Nothing: `CompletableFuture.cancel` never reaches the work behind a future
Their threads are interrupted
They finish, and their results go into the cache
quiz.why: The `future` builder links both ways: the coroutine completes the future, and cancelling the future cancels the coroutine. From there, cancellation travels down to the `supervisorScope` and its `async` children. A future made with `supplyAsync` is the case where the second option holds.

quiz.q: Someone builds `QuoteService`'s scope from `context + Job()` instead of `SupervisorJob()`. One request fails with `NoQuoteException` while 40 others are in flight. What happens?
options: Only that request's future fails
The other 40 are cancelled, the scope is cancelled, and every later request's future comes back cancelled at once
The other 40 finish, but new requests fail
Only requests for the same destination are cancelled
quiz.why: A failed child cancels a plain `Job` parent, and the cancelled parent cancels all its other children. A cancelled scope can't run new coroutines either: each new `future` completes with `JobCancellationException` at once. With `SupervisorJob`, each request's failure stays in its own future.

flashcards.back: `supervisorScope`. Any one answer will do, so a failed call must not cancel the others.

flashcards.front: Why `withTimeoutOrNull` inside each `async`, not one `withTimeout` around the whole fan-out?
flashcards.back: Per call, only the late courier drops out. Around everything, the timeout cancels all calls and throws away answers that already arrived.

flashcards.front: Why is `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` wrong around a courier's `await` in this fan-out?
flashcards.back: A courier's own client timeout throws a `CancellationException` too, so rethrowing it ends the whole request.

flashcards.front: What does `currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()` tell you inside a catch?
flashcards.back: It throws only if your own coroutine was cancelled. If it returns, the cancellation came from the call you awaited.

flashcards.front: What does `cancel(true)` on a future from `scope.future { }` do?
flashcards.back: It cancels the coroutine, and through the job tree, every child the coroutine started.

flashcards.front: Why does `QuoteService` build its scope with `SupervisorJob()`?
flashcards.back: With a plain `Job`, one failed request cancels the scope and every other request, and later futures come back cancelled at once.

flashcards.front: May a stale price refresh the cache?
flashcards.back: No. Only live answers go in; otherwise one old price could be served forever.

terms.plain: A piece of work that can pause without holding its thread, and carry on later where it stopped.
Starting several independent calls at once and combining what comes back.
The time by which a request must answer, whatever the calls behind it do.
A scope whose children fail alone; cancelling the scope still cancels them all.
The last live price for a destination, served and labelled as old when no courier answers in time.
`scope.future { }`: starts a coroutine and returns a `CompletableFuture` linked to it both ways.
The parent and child links between running coroutines; cancellation travels down it.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate asks why `BestQuote` needs `supervisorScope`, `withTimeoutOrNull` on every call and that odd `ensureActive()` in a catch, and what actually stops the courier calls when a client hangs up. Explain it in your own words.
explain_back.answer: A price needs any one courier's answer, not all three, so one courier failing must not cancel the others. In a plain coroutineScope, a failed child cancels its siblings at once, so we use supervisorScope, where each async keeps its failure for await and we turn it into no answer. Each call gets the deadline with withTimeoutOrNull: a late courier becomes null and the others still count, and since all calls start together, the request ends by the deadline. withTimeout would be worse, because its TimeoutCancellationException is a CancellationException, and a courier's own client can throw one too. If we rethrew every CancellationException, one courier's timeout would end the request. So in the catch we call ensureActive: it throws only if our own coroutine was cancelled, and otherwise that courier just has no answer. With no answers, we serve the last live price marked stale, or fail with NoQuoteException. On hang-up, lesson 1's handler cancels the future in channelInactive; scope.future links that future to the request's coroutine, so the coroutine is cancelled and the cancel goes down the job tree to the three courier calls. The service's scope uses SupervisorJob, so one failed request can't cancel the rest.

deeper.body:
Four refinements a production fan-out often adds.

Pass the deadline on. The service knows that a request has, say, 180 ms left; the courier doesn't. Many systems that call each other over a network send the time left along with each call, so that the far side can give up too, instead of finishing work nobody will read. With coroutines you compute it from a start time and pass it down; `withTimeoutOrNull` then wraps the time that is left, not a fixed number.

Answer early when the answer can't get much better. If any price within 10 cents of the lowest seen in the last minute is good enough, the request can return as soon as one such price arrives, and cancel the rest. That is `select` over the `onAwait` clauses (Channels, select and pipelines), with the losers cancelled by hand.

Put an age on the cache. Store the time with each price, and refuse to serve one older than a few minutes. Then a long outage ends in a clear error, not in a price from last week.

Mind the `await` rule. The kotlinx.coroutines KDoc notes that `await()` on a `Deferred` that someone else cancelled throws `CancellationException` in *your* coroutine, even though your coroutine is fine. This lesson's `ensureActive()` check is the documented way to tell the two apart, and it is worth using anywhere you await work you didn't start.

Lesson 3 of this track adds what the fan-out still lacks: a limit on how many calls each courier sees at once, retries for the calls that are safe to repeat, a second call for the slowest courier, and turning work away when the whole service is full.
